See my full review here. —Molly Higgins

Hairmax LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex for $849: Unlike the usual helmet- or hat-based regrowth devices, the Hairmax LaserBand is a 3-inch-thick, flexible headband studded with 82 concentrated lasers rather than LEDs. (There’s also a slimmer, 41-laser version for $250 less.) Take it off its charging cradle and place it on one section of your head for 30 seconds, three times a week. When the time is up, it will buzz loudly; then you can move it to the next section. I appreciated the speedy treatment time, but the headband’s silicone teeth also didn't secure the band in place very well when I was treating my frontal hairline, so I had to stand still while holding it. However, it does work—after five months of testing, I saw definite improvement in growth along my hair part. —Kat Merck

Hooga Red Light Therapy Hat for Hair Growth for $299: I was excited to try this more affordable red-light hat after loving my experience with the HigherDose one, but I found myself unimpressed and actually uncomfortable while using it. The Hooga Red Light Therapy Hat looks like a baseball cap, but it doesn’t have a battery, so you have to stay plugged into the wall the entire time you use it. Feels a little pointless to look outdoor-ready when you can’t actually use it on the go. It also got too hot for me to wear comfortably. —Nena Farrell

Does Red-Light Therapy Work for Hair Loss?

Yes—research suggests low-level light therapy can work for certain types of hair loss, such as androgenetic alopecia, also known as male or female pattern hair loss. It can help increase hair count, thickness, and density by stimulating hair follicles and boosting cellular activity in the scalp.

That said, results depend heavily on the type and severity of hair loss. Red-light therapy works best in cases of mild to moderate thinning and may be less effective for advanced hair loss or scarring conditions like cicatricial alopecia. Consistency also matters. You typically need regular, ongoing use to maintain results, and benefits can diminish if treatments stop.

What Wavelength of Red Light Is Best for Hair Restoration?

According to the American Hair Loss Association, wavelengths in the range of 630 to 680 nanometers are ideal for hair regrowth. These wavelengths are known to support increased blood flow to the scalp, boost cellular activity, and help reduce inflammation. Some clinical studies specifically cite 650 nanometers as an especially effective wavelength.

Red-light devices that use medical-grade laser diodes tend to deliver more targeted and consistent light than standard LEDs, but both can stimulate hair follicles at the right wavelengths. For best results, look for FDA-cleared devices that list their wavelengths and power output.

How to Use Red-Light Therapy for Hair Growth

Consistency is the most important part of any red-light therapy routine. Most devices require at least three months of use before noticeable results are observed, and some may take longer. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions, as treatment schedules vary by device, but most recommend sessions three to five times per week. The hair growth is preserved only with continued use, so you’ll need ongoing maintenance sessions.

Always start with a clean and dry scalp so the light can reach your hair follicles without interference from oils or styling products. Some devices include protective eyewear, and if yours does, wear it during treatment. Make sure to wipe the device down with a gentle disinfectant before or after each session to prevent buildup on the LEDs.

Topical regrowth treatments can complement red-light therapy and may help support thicker hair. A few randomized clinical trials suggest that combining minoxidil (2 percent or 5 percent) with red-light therapy can improve hair density and encourage faster regrowth compared to using either treatment alone. For a natural alternative, some research has found rosemary oil to produce results comparable to 2 percent minoxidil for androgenetic alopecia, though the evidence isn’t as extensive as it is for minoxidil.

If you’re pregnant or have an underlying medical condition, talk to your healthcare provider before starting any form of red-light therapy.

Is Red-Light Therapy for Hair Growth Safe?

Yes—for most people, red-light therapy is considered a safe and noninvasive treatment with minimal side effects when used as intended. Still, it's always worth consulting a health care professional before starting any sort of treatment. This is especially the case for anyone with photosensitive conditions or autoimmune disorders that affect light sensitivity.

I prefer devices that are FDA-cleared because it means they've met certain safety standards for consumer use. But keep in mind that the clearance process is less rigorous than the FDA approval pathway, as it just requires manufacturers to prove their product is “substantially equivalent” to an already legally marketed device. Also, FDA clearance isn't a guarantee of results; it simply means it's considered safe to use as directed at home.

#377. Start a game night tradition with these Black Friday board game deals

Looking to start up a board game night tradition? Well, Black Friday week is the perfect time to host the inaugural event, with price drops across all kinds of games — from family games to hardcore strategy brain-teasers — in Amazon's Black Friday sale.

A board game isn't just the perfect thing to add to your arsenal of entertainment items at home. It's also a good gift idea for a hard-to-shop-for relative, older kids, or family who just doesn't want or need anything else — not to mention the potential for lots of fun with family and friends over Thanksgiving and Christmas.

Board games — or "table top gaming", to give it a proper name — is having a moment, which means there are lots of new and innovative titles available. There are twists on classics as well as ingenious new concepts. Don't worry if you're a bit lost in the gaming world, when it comes to board games we know our stuff, and we've combed the Black Friday listings to find you the best discounted games.

Here are the best Black Friday board game deals we've found so far. Keep checking back, however, as new deals will be added as Black Friday week rolls on.

There's a current trend for deception games, partly driven by the popularity of TV's The Traitors. Chameleon sees a group of players take turn to describe a word or concept without actually saying it. But one player is actually the Chameleon and has to guess the word from the other players' clues — all while avoiding detection. It's a ridiculous amount of fun, and perfect for big groups and players of all ages.

Catan is a veritable board game classic, and it's a great pick to snag while it's discounted. Three to four players settle a randomly laid-out island, collecting wood, brick, wool, grain, and ore to build roads, settlements, and cities. Games wrap up in about an hour to 90 minutes, and it's fairly easy to learn. And if you're tired of playing the same things over and over, Catan's modular board means no two games set up the same way. It's a significant upgrade from Monopoly that's suitable for the whole family.

The classics are classic for a reason. Mouse Trap has delighted kids and families for years, and nothing has changed after all this time. Indeed, it's as fiddly to set up as it ever was, but there's no denying the fun of setting the trap in motion. Kids will love the mechanics, parents will love the nostalgia. You can also find Black Friday discounts on other kids classics, including Connect 4, Battleship, and Candy Land.

If you've ever wanted to get started with Dungeons & Dragons but didn't know how, this board game is the perfect introduction. It has a quick-start guide, player boards for the Cleric, Rogue, Wizard, and Fighter, and cards for species, backgrounds, spells, and gear so nobody has to build a character from scratch. Three to five players run through three adventure booklets split between combat, exploration, and roleplaying, and the poster maps for the Keep and the Caves of Chaos pull from one of the oldest modules in the game’s history. It's got everything beginners need and then some, so it's a much less daunting introductory experience.

If you haven't played the Horrified series, it's worth checking out for team-based beast-slaying. Players join forces to take on various classic monster — in this version it's American monsters that include Bigfoot, the Jersey Devil, and Mothman — with different ways of killing each monster. Board game fans will be familiar with the mechanics of the gameplay but the great thing about it is that you can mix and match the monsters, so each time you play is different. It can also get pretty tense as you ratchet up the difficulty level. #376. Russian helicopter suspected of violating Finnish airspace

Finland's Defense Ministry thinks the incursion is linked to a drone strike earlier Saturday on a Russian cargo ship, which is on a US sanctions list.

A Russian helicopter is suspected of violating Finnish airspace, the Nordic country's Ministry of Defense said Saturday.

The incident happened a few hours after a drone attack left a Russian cargo ship ablaze in the Gulf of Finland, the easternmost part of the Baltic Sea.

According to Finland's Defense Ministry, the incursion happened at 12:34 p.m. local time (10:34 UTC/GMT) off the town of Loviisa, on the southern coast.

"This alleged airspace violation may be linked to rescue or surveillance operations carried out by Finland following damage sustained by a cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland," public broadcaster YLE cited Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen as saying.

The ministry added the helicopter could have penetrated up to 4.1 kilometers (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory.

Earlier Saturday, Finland — one of NATO's newest members — said a Russian cargo ship heading for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad caught fire after being struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland.

The Finnish military said the Sparta II was damaged ⁠west ⁠of Russia's Gogland island, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Finland's coast, and later drifted into Finnish territorial waters.

Finnish ‌Border ​Guard Commander Ilja Iljin later told YLE that the vessel, which is known to have links to the Russian military, was struck by Ukrainian  drones while in Russian waters.

"At the moment, ​there is no confirmed information ⁠about ​what cargo ​is on board, ​but it ‌cannot be ruled out ​that ⁠there is military materiel on ⁠board," ​Iljin said.

The ship is on a US sanctions list, according to a search of the Open Sanctions website.

The Border Guard later said the crew of the Sparta II was evacuating into a life raft and rescue boat.

"The [Ukraine] war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas," wrote Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on X.

Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor," he added.

The Finnish government has put temporary curbs on aviation and maritime traffic in the eastern Gulf of Finland.

The Defense Ministry said Finland had informed its allies about the incident.

Black Friday is here again — one of the great holiday shopping traditions. We have our own tradition here at Mashable: making a beeline for the MacBook deals in Amazon's Black Friday sale. For most of the year, Apple prices are what they are, so it's always exciting to see just how heavily MacBooks are discounted for Black Friday.

If you're in the market for the lighter, slimmer, more portable MacBook Air, you're in luck. Amazon has slashed prices across the 2026 range, with savings of up to $300. #373. The 6 Best Latte Machines for Automatic Espresso Drinks (2026)

A latte is rich and milky heaven. A cappuccino is the cloud that heaven rests on. The best latte machines and the best automatic espresso machines are the ones that can give you this richness consistently, easily, and deliciously. Home espresso machines, like the classic devices in our guide to the Best Espresso Machines, often have a reputation for being intimidating. But they don't have to be.

Some machines make it easy and keep you from having to drive to the coffee shop. The automatic espresso machines in this guide can make a perfect frothy cappuccino accessible with the press of a single button, or maybe a couple of buttons. Our top high-end superautomatic espresso machine, the De'Longhi Rivelia (7/10, WIRED Recommends), is a paragon of easy-peasy, frothy, pleasing cappuccinos and flat whites. The new Ninja Cafe Luxe Pro (see here on Amazon) seems determined to produce every kind of coffee in existence.

Most of the machines on this list also come with grinders, but our guide to The Best Coffee Grinders may also be helpful. For more WIRED coffee coverage, check out our guides to The Best Coffee Subscriptions, The Best Drip Coffee Machines, The Best Milk Frothers, and The Best Cold Brew Makers, or look for our recent coffee gear reviews.

Updated November 2026: We’ve added information on WIRED UK’s blind taste test of popular fully automatic bean-to-cup machines and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

A sophisticated bean-to-cup machine from Italian coffee titan De'Longhi, the Rivelia (7/10, WIRED Recommends) immediately ranks among the most modern, impressive, user-friendly, and capable superautomatic espresso machines I’ve encountered—the sort that has you dump a half-bag of beans into a hopper and will grind, brew, then froth up milk for a flat white, amid 18 options on espresso, latte, cappuccino, and iced-coffee drink options.

Pretty much everything operates via an easy touchscreen, including bean guidance that lets you optimize the machine for each bean. The milk frother works at the press of a button and makes actual microfoam—and the foam’s density can be adjusted to make a frothier cappuccino or dense flat white. It’s so easy I let my parents test-drive it, and they fell in love with it within a day. If you’ve got multiple people using the machine, you can save multiple profiles and your favorite custom drinks. So Dad can have his basic “coffee” that’s actually a European-style café crema, and Mom can have her ridiculously large 16-ounce travel-mug latte. (Yes, these are their drinks.)

What's better, the Rivelia has two swappable bean hoppers, so it’s easy to swap between caff and decaf, or between light and dark roasts. Honestly, this is the bean-to-cup espresso machine that fully sold me on the idea of automatic coffee machines like this one. Though note: Fully automatic espresso machines like the Rivelia grind a little coarser, in order to make espresso less finicky and less difficult. This leads to a smoother but less nuanced profile than espresso shots you’d find in a café. But if you're a milk lover, the absolute ease with which the Rivelia froths a cappuccino will likely balance this out. The cold espresso is also a pleasant option when mixed with milk or vodka.

A lot of machines can make you a cloudy, clumpy, big-bubble cappuccino without much hassle. But it's that well-integrated microfoam, the silkiness, that feels like an actual luxury—elevates a good foamed milk from the merely milky latte to silly morning ecstasy.

There's a lot to like about Ninja's flagship entry into the espresso market: in particular, dosing by weight and an easy bean guidance function that actually helps in dialing in a bean. Quite simply, this machine offers real-deal, unpressurized portafilter espresso without the fussiness. But what I especially like about this Ninja is the milk. Some superautomatic machines have tube-filled, plasticky milk systems that are annoying to clean. Some never get a fine froth. This Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro is the best of each world, a steam wand and stainless steel steamer cup with a spinning whisk at its bottom that simulates the whirlpool created by a skilled barista. Whether cold foam or hot foam, Ninja's Luxe Cafe series offers truly excellent foam for your morning cup.

Now, for this: It is not a superautomatic machine like the Rivelia, though it’s among the easiest portafilter machines I've ever used. The conical burr grinder is built in, it doses accurately, the tamper handle is easy, and bean guidance will tell you what to do without much fuss. Mostly, you just need to transfer the portafilter from one spot on the machine to another.

Note that for a lower price, the Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier (described below) offers the same great milk froth, but you lose the automatic tamper and a hot water spout. For me, the Pro is the pick for a more pleasant morning and greater versatility. Note that while the massive drip tray does hold a lot of water, it’s a bit of a production to empty and replace, and that while it also purports to be a drip coffee maker, it’s nothing to write your mother about.

This Mr. Coffee machine was once our top pick for lattes. Why? Because it sits so nicely at a comfortable intersection where ease of use meets automation and affordability. This is about the lowest-priced machine you can ever expect to find with automatic milk frothing at the press of a single button, with options for latte foam or cappuccino froth. Just load fine-ground coffee into the portafilter, tamp it down, and twist it on. The machine will mix up a cappuccino or a latte macchiato at the press of a button.

This machine has a forgiving (but not overly intense or nuanced) pressurized portafilter, which means it will work with almost any “espresso-grind” coffee from your local café or the grocery store. Just note you’ll still get a better shot of espresso if you buy a grinder and use fresh beans from a good specialty roaster. But all in all, this is about the easiest $200 latte machine we know. Like, the hardest thing about it is that the milk canister can be removed and stored in the fridge, and you have to clean it out once a week.

The Cafe Affetto is one of the few fully automatic machines that WIRED has enjoyed in this price range. The Affetto features a built-in steaming wand, produces 20 bars of pump pressure to ensure your espresso is fully extracted, and is a slick little machine. It’s very slim and fits comfortably on a small apartment countertop without having to rearrange everything. Because coffee production is automated, you just need to fill the water tank and put whole beans in the hopper, and you’re good to go. You can brew one or two shots with just the press of a button, and there’s a programmable button to create your favorite drinks (like an Americano with just the right amount of water).

The milk frother does a lot of the work on its own. Just pour some of your favorite milk into the frothing pitcher, submerge the wand, and hit the steam button. If you’re new to frothing milk, you don't even need to move the pitcher to produce a creamy and consistent microfoam. WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey tested the frother with dairy milk, oat milk, and soy milk, and found it produced soft and creamy café-grade froth each time. Just make sure it’s topped up with water and beans and that you clean out the spent grounds container regularly, and it works like a dream.

The Breville Oracle Jet (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is my favorite of the two dozen or so new espresso machines I’ve tried so far this year. It’s the one I recommend as my top pick in WIRED’s guide to the Best Espresso Machines, over other estimable contenders from Breville that include the Barista Touch ($1,000) and the Barista Pro ($850). And it’s the one that best mixes full-flavored, nuanced espresso with the ease of machine-guided, touchscreen operation. It’s versatile, it’s powerful, its PID controller means the brew temperature is quite stable, and it makes absolutely lovely cups—espresso that’s denser and more intensely aromatic than the coffee made by any other machine on this list, whether in bringing out the fruity berry notes in an anaerobic light roast or the dark chocolate of a roasty Italian.

In the finicky, often difficult world of classic home espresso machines, the Oracle Jet is a paragon of simplicity and machine-guided brewing: It’s a miracle that one can so easily pull such delicious and nuanced shots that remain so sensitive to the character of each bean. But that sensitivity still makes the Oracle Jet a little more finicky than other machines on this list. And while the automatic milk frothing is quite good, it’s not as failsafe as our favorites here. (I still like steaming milk manually on the Breville, versus using the auto-froth.)

Which is to say that as a latte machine, this Breville is all about the espresso. If you want espresso that will distill the beauteous character of fresh-roasted beans but still don't want to try overly hard—on a machine whose intuitive touchscreen tutorial will guide you to lovely flat whites and capps? This is your huckleberry.

For those who’d rather not fuss with beans at all but still want a lovely milk-frothed latte and cappuccino in the morning, there is this clever two-piece setup from Nespresso—with “espresso” on one machine via Vertuo coffee pods and an Aeroccino milk frother that’s whisper-quiet and will whip you up some milk foam in a minute. The espresso that comes from pods is not quite espresso, of course, but WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe loved it best of all pod espresso machines, with excellent body and mouthfeel and especially ease. The Vertuo Pop+ will also make a drip-coffee-style mug.

But this frother bundle generally offers you a good bargain on an all-in-one system, and the Aeroccino is in the upper echelon of milk frothers WIRED has tested. (Note, however, you'll have to plug in each machine separately.) This said, if you want the ease of pod espresso but are fussy about your milk, you may want to grab a stand-alone Vertuo Pop+ ($129) and the excellent Dreo Baristamaker ($100). Do this when a good sale is running, and you might cobble this together at a similar price to the Aeroccino bundle.

The Aeroccino was easy to use—pour in your milk of choice and press the button. it will heat and froth your milk automatically—it takes about a minute, and it’s whisper-quiet. Every Nespresso capsule I’ve tried has featured a thick layer of crema, and having whipped, thick milk on top of it made my average cup of coffee a more elevated experience.

Sometimes making a whole latte or cappuccino using an automated machine can be a time suck. Not to mention, sometimes all you really want is frothy milk. That’s where milk frothers come in. These machines beat air into milk, or milk substitutes, to get that nice creamy froth. Former WIRED Reviewer Jaina Grey loved this handheld from Subminimal, a highly specialized immersion blender that makes properly textured, creamy, light, airy, wonderful milk. One screen makes fine-textured milk. One makes “ultra-fine.” Note that Subminimal has also added a milk frothing pitcher called the Nanofoamer Pro ($159) that costs a bit more, but is currently sitting prettily atop our guide to the Best Milk Frothers.

This streamlined machine from relative newcomer Terra Kaffe is a pleasant surprise, given the complexity of Terra Kaffe's first machine, the superautomatic TK-02 (see below), which bristled with features and doohickeys. The Demi is perhaps the dead-simplest fully automatic espresso machine I've yet encountered that still makes good coffee. If you don't want to customize your shot, there's just a dial and a button: espresso, lungo, Americano, drip, hot water, bye!

You can click into submenus and edit these to a nerd's content, both by volume and strength. You can adjust among five grinder settings as well—a low but relatively typical number of settings for automatic machines that already grind coarser than espresso machines with portafilters. You may need to futz with grind and dose strength to get good results with light roast, especially on espresso, but with a good medium roast, the Terra Kaffe offers a very smooth ride. Honestly, this is the machine I'd put in a front room for customers to use if I owned a small business. Super easy, no fuss, good for multiple types of people—and the reservoir is big enough at 1.4 liters that you won't be refilling the water all day.

But note that this is actually not a latte machine: It's only half of one. There's no milk frother. Luckily, the world is full of good milk frothing jugs these days, and we especially recommend the Subminimal Nanofoamer Pro ($159), WIRED's favorite milk frother.

Ninja has a habit of taking high-falutin', pro-level, or commercial equipment—whether soft-serve ice cream machines or slushie machines—and finding a way to make it easy, accessible, fun, and probably viral on TikTok. WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane was skeptical about Ninja's first foray into the latte and cappuccino world with the Luxe Cafe Premier (7/10, WIRED Recommends), especially since the machine also promised cold brew and even traditional drip coffee. But she came away impressed.

This Ninja is not a superautomatic machine like our top automated pick, the Rivelia. It's what the industry likes to call “semiautomatic.” Semiautomatic espresso machines offer a built-in grinder and automatic milk frother but still use a non-pressurized portafilter that will pull a classic espresso shot with full nuance and aromatics. In our espresso maker guide, we recommend the ever-reliable and terrific Breville Barista Express ($700) as WIRED's favorite accessibly priced semiautomatic. But this Ninja is the machine I'd probably give to a beginner, a new college grad, or anyone whose first priority is ease and great automatically foamed milk

The drip coffee is meh, granted. But more than perhaps any semiautomatic machine in its price range, the Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier is geared to absolute ease and versatility—with an intuitive digital user interface that helps you along. Depending on your chosen drink, the Ninja Luxe will recommend the appropriate grind size on its display screen and help you dial it in. (This may take a couple of tries.) Milk frothing is easy, and the automatic milk frothing is shockingly good. Plus, you can froth cold foam, for silly cold-foam drinks. See what I mean? Ninja is fun. That said, we ended up preferring the Luxe Cafe Pro ($750), which costs a little more but adds a welcome auto-tamper and hot water spout.

This superautomatic espresso machine is one of the few coffee machines made by German auto and appliance behemoth Bosch. It is both highly sophisticated and a bit of an odd duck—capable of making an unholy variety of espresso drinks downloaded via firmware. The milk system is especially interesting, and for some, it may be the biggest selling point. On the base model, the milk system is basically a tube you attach to the side of the brew head. You can stick the other end of the tube in any container, and it'll steam whatever milk you've got directly into your cup before adding the espresso. This is great for families who use multiple milks. It's also great for not wasting milk.

The espresso is similar to superautomatics from De'Longhi, which is to say it's a smoother, more rounded, but less nuanced take on espresso that's great for milk drinks. But the “drip” is also interesting. The Bosch 800 “slow brew” coffee—while it does not have the clarity or brightness of drip coffee— is perhaps my favorite drip coffee from an espresso machine, round and roasty and lovely. It extracts only the smooth, chocolate end of the coffee spectrum. I haven't tested the pH, but it seems quite low in acidity. It's nice.

But here are the caveats: Coffee cup height clearance can be an issue on milk drinks, the pump is a bit louder than some, it's slow to boot up, and some parts feel a bit flimsy or plasticky for a machine in this price range. Also, if you do want an attached milk carafe, it's hundreds of dollars more, depending on current deals.

The delta between home espresso machines and the commercial workhorses used by busy third-wave shops is still thousands of dollars, but that hasn’t stopped both beloved brands and scrappy upstarts from infiltrating the space with more approachable units. Skip the junk and level up to the Casabrews 5700PRO (7/10, WIRED Review), which offers an unfussy take on the art of homemade espresso drinks.

Instead of bewildering noobs with a million settings and onboard tutorials, this 12 x 11 x 16-inch tank of a machine keeps it simple with easily accessible controls for things like temperature and dose volume for extraction, and run time for the onboard grinder. It's a single-boiler machine, not a dual boiler, which means you can’t froth your latte milk at the same time as pulling a shot, but the texture of the frothed milk is perfectly malleable and up to snuff for a basic leaf or rosetta pattern.

The guide rails that hold the portafilter in place are a bit too close to the output spout of the grinder, and temperature controls that deal in absolute rather than relative values would be welcome improvements. But until Casabrews implements our feedback, this is still a solid unit that’s a great pick for anyone who’s ready to never leave their house for a cappuccino ever again. —Pete Cottell

The superautomatic Terra Kaffe is a pricey hunk of machinery and has its bugs, but considering its ease and customizability, it's worth the price, wrote WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane last year. She praised the device's convenience, its ease, the front-facing water filter, waste tray, and milk carafe, and its excellent app (available for iOs and Android) that offers easy controls and the ability to warm up your machine from your bed or the bathroom.

Drinks like latte macchiatos, drips, and iced coffee can all be adjusted to your tastes, and a milk frothing dial allows you to adjust the milk’s texture from foamy to silky. For those who love true, real, drip coffee, that's the biggest selling point for the Terra Kaffe over our top automated picks, the De'Longhi Rivelia and the Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier: The TK-02 offers it. The drip coffee is also good enough that Shane cleared her Chemex pour-over carafe from her counter.

De’Longhi’s Magnifica Start is a no-nonsense superautomatic with a conical burr grinder, four preset recipes at the push of a button, and the ability to brew a smooth and potent espresso, wrote WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane. As with other high-end De'Longhi devices of the moment, the milk frother is truly impressive, offering seriously luxurious frothed milk. Milk-based recipes at the touch of a button are a latte macchiato and a cappuccino, while espresso and Americanos are the espresso-based options. There’s a slot for ground beans and a hopper for whole beans. Figuring out grind size takes a little trial and error, Shane noted, and it's not an overly quiet machine. But the Start is compact and efficient, and priced far lower than our favorite De'Longhi automatic, the Rivelia. This makes the Magnifica Start a solid investment.

The key here is automation. We wanted to test machines that make you a cup of coffee with a single touch, or as close to that as possible. So the products on this list are all of the automatic and semiautomatic variety. You fill ’em up and they do all the hard work—or most of it, anyway. Nothing here doesn't have a milk frother that does the work by itself.

Setup and cleanup were especially important, as was durability. The entire point of a device like this is to save time and energy and/or produce a drink of higher quality than can be made without it, so we didn’t recommend any products that didn’t produce tasty espresso and save time.

In May 2026, WIRED’s UK team gathered four fully automatic machines—the Terra Kaffe TK-02 (above), Philips’ Café Aromis 8000 Series, De'Longhi's Eletta Explore, and Jura E8—and made both lattes and espressos for local industry experts to judge. You can read the results and watch the resulting video here. The Reviews team is currently testing the winner of that challenge, Philips Café Aromis 8000, to see how it compares against the top picks in this guide.

Even if you're not making espresso, the first and best thing you can do to dramatically improve your morning coffee is to buy locally roasted beans. Plug your city or region and “locally roasted coffee beans” into Google and you will be glad you did. The reason that your locally roasted coffee will taste worlds better than anything you'd buy from a major coffee roaster (like Starbucks, Illy, or Gevalia) is simple: Good coffee starts to lose flavor the moment it's roasted. Get it fresh and you're giving yourself a much better chance at high-quality espresso.

Want some help finding the best roasters? For some of our favorite mail-order brands, with beans often roasted the same day or week they're placed in the mail, check out our roundup of the Best Coffee Subscription Services.

I hate to break it to you, but pre-ground coffee from a supermarket bag is pretty much always worse. Unless you see a roasting date on the bag, you probably have no idea when the roaster actually roasted it. If the roaster is a French or Italian brand, there's a good chance it was months ago. Coffee is best when it's fresh, ideally brewed a week or two after it's roasted. And grinding the beans dramatically increases the rate at which coffee degrades. This doesn't just affect how the coffee tastes. It affects how well the espresso maker will push water through the beans, leading to possible blowouts or bad extraction.

If you haven’t made espresso before and you don't have access to a coffee grinder, we recommend you buy locally roasted beans. Just ask your local coffee roaster for a fine (espresso) grind. We've tried a lot of pre-ground espresso blends from popular companies like Lavazza, Gevalia, and Café Bustelo. They were all very dark and very bitter, partially because they are all either imported or roasted in big batches and shipped all over the world. Pre-ground coffee will always be a little stale, and it's hard to get a good cup from coffee that's started to degrade—which happens fast after you grind it.

Get it ground fresh from a local roaster, and you'll have about a two-week window before you'll notice any difference. Many of the machines recommended here come with a grinder, so whole beans are already the best choice. But our roundup of The Best Coffee Grinders can also provide some guidance here, if you want to get into the grinding game, buy whole beans, and keep your coffee tasting its best.

Look, milk is milk. Anything that contains milk has the potential to get strange over time, and this includes the milk containers and milk frothers on automatic espresso machines. WIRED's previous espresso reviewer, Jaina Grey, was extremely sensitive to this issue—devoting her time to dishwashering, soaping, scrubbing, and otherwise testing the best methods for making sure that milk containers on automatic espresso machines remain sacrosanct environments.

Regular washing is, of course, the first and best recourse. But occasionally, you'll also want to sterilize your milk reservoir and milk frother.

First, hand-wash it with soap and water as usual, and make sure you get a sponge into those corners. Next up, there are a couple of options. The most effective will be a food-grade sanitizer like Star San, or One Step. Essentially, just make a dilution per the instructions on either product, pour that into a spray bottle, give the inside of the milk container a couple of sprays, and let it dry on a drying rack.

The second-best option, the one that uses things you probably have in your house right now, is a mix of distilled white vinegar and plain old tap water. If you have staining or really stubborn smells, you'll want to let it soak. Try adding about one shot glass (1.5 ounces) of distilled white vinegar and fill the container up the rest of the way with warm water. Let it soak for about 30 minutes, then rinse it out till there's no more vinegar smell, and you should be good to go.

#372. Germany news: IG Metall union calls for new 24-hour strike

Germany's biggest single union, IG Metall, is calling on car and shipyard workers to strike amid a pay row. Meanwhile, Germany's president is setting off on an Africa trip. DW has more.

This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of headlines from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 21, and Sunday, November 22, 2026:

Bosses at soccer team Bayern Munich have publicly questioned whether young Germany international Jamal Musiala's contract is valid in view of a debilitating neurological condition.

The remarks have been criticized by media and from several other quarters, among them the global players' union FIFPRO, which accused the officials of neglecting their "duty of care" toward their players.

You can read details on what has been happening at the top football club in this DW article: Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments

Friedrich Christian "Mick" Flick, an art collector, investor and multimillionaire who belonged to one of Germany's richest business dynasties, has died aged 82 in Rosenheim in the southern state of Bavaria, his family has said.

The family said in a statement issued on Saturday that Flick left behind "the memory of a life shaped by significant acts of generosity as a donor and patron, particularly in contemporary art and in promoting tolerance."

Flick was the grandson of Friedrich Flick, who made a huge fortune in the Nazi era with his coal and steel business, partly by using forced labor.

This past came back to haunt the grandson in 2003 when he pledged to loan his world-famous collection of modern art to Berlin, with the Central Council of Jews in Germany calling the Flick Collection a "Göring Collection" and saying the loan was intended to wash clean the "blood money" from the Nazi era.

The collection, which contains some 2,500 works by 150 artists, was exhibited in parts in the German capital from 2004 to 2021.

Flick later said in an interview that the widespread outrage, while hurtful, had forced him to look more closely at his family's history.

According to his family, Flick once said: "I have no guilt for my forefathers' conduct, but I feel a responsibility, a very special responsibility. Every German bears this responsibility. As a Flick, I bear it twice."

Among other things, he collaborated with the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, which oversees Berlin's museums, to research his family's Nazi past.

He also set up a foundation in Potsdam, near Berlin, that aimed to combat xenophobia and racism and contributed €5 million ($5.4 million) to the foundation to compensate former forced laborers.

The family was also involved in a highly publicized party donations scandal in the 1980s that became known as the "Flick Affair."

"Mick" Flick married Countess Maya von Schönburg (1958-2019), the older sister of well-known socialite, businesswoman, art collector and artist Gloria von Thurn und Taxis, in 1985. The couple had three children.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is setting off on a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya.

Steinmeier will be accompanied by a business delegation and is expected to focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers during the trip.

On Monday, Steinmeier is to be received by Ivorian President Allassane Outtara in Abidjan, Ivory Coast's largest city and seat of government.

The next day, in the Ghanaian capital, Accra, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which, according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa."

On Wednesday, he will be received by Kenyan President William Ruto in Nairobi.

In Kenya, Steinmeier will also visit the Crescent Island Game Sanctuary on Thursday, the last day of his trip.

The Federal Institute for Hydrology (BfG) has said it expects water levels in large rivers in western Germany, including the Rhine, to return to average or above in the next few days amid sustained rainfall.

It said the water level at the key gauge in Kaub near Koblenz, located at an important bottleneck on the Middle Rhine, could reach some 3.3 meters (10.8 feet), more than 3 meters higher than the last recorded low-water readings.

The BfG said it also expected rising water levels in the Weser and Danube rivers, with smaller increases in the Elbe and Oder.

The rising water level in the Rhine, an important shipping route, means that conditions for water-borne cargo transport have improved, according to Germany's inland navigation association BDB.

"The more abundant rainfall in the past days has caused the water level in the Rhine to rise considerably, and they will keep rising a great deal in the next few days as well, meaning that each ship has much more transport capacity again," said Fabian Spiess, the deputy manager at BDB.

In the middle of the year, many ships were forced to drastically reduce the loads they carried, leading to economic losses that will not be recuperated any time soon, according to Spiess.

He cited the year 2018, in which shipping on the Rhine was also hindered by extremely low water levels, saying that the months of improved conditions at the end of that year had not been enough to make good the economic damage incurred.

The conservation NGO also said that the current rain provided temporary relief to the environment but could not compensate for the negative consequences of the long dry period.

It said species of animals, such as amphibians and water insects, that lived in small bodies of water and moist habitats had been particularly impacted.

Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig says that she intends to tighten the law on murders committed with "gender-specific" motives, with a particular focus on femicides perpetrated by men who are unable to accept a separation or the desire of a woman to live a self-determined life.

"A man kills, or attempts to kill, his partner or ex-partner almost every day in Germany," Hubig told the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild newspaper.

"Any man killing a woman because she wants to leave him must be punished as a murderer," she said, noting that in some cases, courts cite a man's deep sadness or fear of losing a partner to someone else as extenuating circumstances. This can lead to a lesser conviction of manslaughter.

She said that in future, courts should look more closely at such motives to determine whether they were based on sentiments of patriarchal possessiveness.

However, Hubig, who belongs to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), said she was opposed to making femicide a separate category of crime, as some women's rights organizations have demanded.

She said that, in her opinion, doing so would have "no advantages over what we are intending — and much bigger disadvantages."

The proposals are currently being debated within the coalition government and are expected to be presented to the states and associations for consideration before the end of the year.

They will then have to go before the Cabinet before being put before the parliament.

The powerful IG Metall union said on Sunday it would call another 24-hour strike on Monday as a pay dispute continues.

Altogether, some 23,000 workers at 19 companies in northern Germany have been called upon to participate, including employees at automaker Mercedes-Benz, shipbuilding company Meyer Werft and wind ​energy company Siemens Gamesa.

The union said that a strike on Friday saw some 12,300 workers walk out at 17 facilities.

It says that the strikes are meant to increase the pressure on employers to yield to its demands, which include a 5% ‌wage increase.

So far, employers have ⁠offered a one-off payment next year and a 1.3% wage increase from July 2028.

The DW newsroom says "Willkommen!" once more to all its readers as we resume our reporting on all things German.

Some good news is on the agenda: The Rhine River, which we can see from the window of our Bonn office, has recovered after a long period with little rainfall, meaning that the barges plying the waterway can load up properly again.

In other stories, the German president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, is setting off on a trip to Africa, during which he is set to visit three countries with a businesss delegation in tow.

And Germany's powerful IG Metall union has said it is launching another 24-hour strike on Monday amid an escalating pay dispute.

Read on to find out more about what is happening in Germany on Sunday, November 22.

We're pausing our Germany news blog for now. Come back for more on Sunday!

A new goal celebration was devised by Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha after his previous one caused controversy due to its religious aspect.

After scoring the goal that secured Dortmund's 1-0 victory over Borussia Mönchengladbach (see entry below), Nmecha knelt on one knee and crossed his arms in front of his chest. He then spread his arms, appearing to pray with his eyes closed.

Nmecha told broadcaster Sky that he intends to continue expressing his faith during goal celebrations, adding that he had once again given glory to Jesus.

However, he did not perform the controversial part of his usual goal celebration. In it, he removes an imaginary crown from his head and places it on the pitch in front of him while kneeling.

This celebration has been heavily criticized, even by Dortmund's fan department.

Nmecha explained that the celebrations is about "putting down my 'crown' in front of the soon-to-come king and point out to Jesus, my hope and my strength."

The gesture is used by Ballers in God, a network of Christian football players that has been criticized for the homophobic and queerphobic statements made by its members.

Dortmund president Hans-Joachim Watzke said he asked the player not to do the celebration again.

Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha led his team to the top of the German Bundesliga table with a 1-0 victory over last-place Borussia Mönchengladbach.

Meanwhile, Bayern Munich was held to a 1-1 draw at home by Cologne on Friday, and striker Harry Kane suffered a serious ankle injury. The Ballon d'Or winner is set to miss several months after undergoing ankle surgery earlier on Saturday.

Now, Dortmund has 24 points after 10 games, putting them two points ahead of Bayern and third-place Freiburg, who defeated Elversberg 1-0.

Fourth-place RB Leipzig had five different players score in a 5-1 victory over Union Berlin, bringing them to 21 points. Bayer Leverkusen scored four unanswered goals against Paderborn to stay in fifth place.

Germany is seeking to redress years of underinvestment by pouring billions into the modernization of public infrastructure and digital networks, and the transition to renewable energy sources.

But will the plan bring real change amid the labor shortages, burdensome bureaucracy and low productivity currently besetting Europe's largest economy?

DW takes a look at what is one of Germany's biggest public investment drives in decades in this video:

Bundesliga powerhouse Bayern Munich concluded the 2025-26 financial year with record figures.

According to the financial report released Saturday at the club's annual general meeting, the club's total turnover was €988.2 million ($1.08 billion) — that is around €10 million more than the previous year.

Operating profit (EBITDA) increased from €187.8 million to €190.8 million. Pre-tax profit was €35.3 million, and net profit for the year was €22.8 million.

Bayern had a particularly strong year in terms of sponsorships. Turnover increased by nearly €30 million, reaching €268.4 million. The club also set a record in merchandise sales, earning €152.8 million.

"We have achieved another record year," CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen said. "This shows that our club has a strong foundation. And we continue to invest to ensure the best possible conditions for the sporting success of our teams."

Moreover, Bayern achieved another milestone. They reached 500,000 members — more than any other club in the world.

Over the past 12 years, the German giants have doubled their membership, growing from 250,000 in 2014 to 500,000 this year.

"Record champions, record members, record member champions," president Herbert Hainer said.

Members hold a 70% stake in the club, which is well above the simple majority required by German rules.

The remaining 30% is owned by four German companies with roots in Bavaria: Adidas, Audi, Allianz, and Viessmann.

Bayern won the league and cup double in the 2025-26 season, losing only three of 53 games across all competitions. In Europe, the club made it to the Champions League semifinals.

Two and a half weeks after his sudden death, Free Voters leader Hubert Aiwanger, who was Bavarian Minister of Economic Affairs and Deputy Minister-President, was laid to rest in his hometown of Inkofen in Lower Bavaria.

A memorial service was held at the Parish Church of the Presentation of the Lord and broadcast on a screen outside.  According to the organizers, around 2,000 people attended the solemn service.

Aiwanger's funeral was open to the public. His longtime partner, Tanja Schweiger, the Regensburg district administrator (Free Voters), stated that Aiwanger had been "a man of the people."

For that reason, she said, everyone "who liked and appreciated him" was warmly welcome. The politician had already been honored with a state funeral in Munich a week earlier.

Aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel on November 4 after canceling an appointment for health reasons. The 55-year-old died of natural causes.

Harry Kane, Bayern Munich's star striker, has pledged to return to the field for the important matches at the end of the current campaign after undergoing surgery for a torn ankle ligament.

"I'll be back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season," he wrote on social media above a photo of himself on his hospital bed, also thanking fans for their messages of support.

Kane, 33, was injured around 20 minutes into Bayern's 1-1 home draw with Cologne in their Bundesliga match on Friday.

Bayern issued a statement on Saturday saying that Kane had "successfully undergone surgery" on his left ankle but was expected to be out for three to four months.

England captain Kane, who finished the 2025–26 season with over 70 goals for club and country, was awarded the Ballon d'Or for his efforts.

Hubert Aiwanger, the deputy premier and economy minister of the southern state of Bavaria, is being buried on Saturday in his native town of Inkofen.

Aiwanger, the federal leader of the Free Voters (FW) party, died suddenly two weeks ago of natural causes at the age of 55 in a hotel in Berlin.

The funeral service ahead of the burial was open to the public, with police saying they expected some 1,000 participants.

A memorial service was held in Munich a week ago to honor Aiwanger.

#370. The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career

Editor’s Note:  This story was originally published in April 2023.

Slumped on his club, head buried in his arm, Rory McIlroy looked on the verge of tears.

The then-21-year-old had just watched his ball sink into the waters of Rae’s Creek at Augusta National and with it, his dream of winning The Masters, a dream that had looked so tantalizingly close mere hours earlier.

As a four-time major winner and one of the most decorated names in the sport’s history, few players would turn down the chance to swap places with McIlroy heading into Augusta this week.

Yet on Sunday afternoon of April 10, 2011, not a golfer in the world would have wished to be in the Northern Irishman’s shoes.

A fresh-faced, mop-headed McIlroy had touched down in Georgia for the first major of the season with a reputation as the leading light of the next generation of stars.

An excellent 2010 had marked his best season since turning pro three years earlier, highlighted by a first PGA Tour win at the Quail Hollow Championship and a crucial contribution to Team Europe’s triumph at the Ryder Cup.

Yet despite a pair of impressive top-three finishes at the Open and PGA Championship respectively, a disappointing missed cut at The Masters – his first at a major – served as ominous foreshadowing.

McIlroy shot 74 and 77 to fall four strokes short of the cut line at seven-over par, a performance that concerned him enough to take a brief sabbatical from competition.

But one year on in 2011, any lingering Masters demons looked to have been exorcised as McIlroy flew round the Augusta fairways.

Having opened with a bogey-free seven-under 65 – the first time he had ever shot in the 60s at the major – McIlroy pulled ahead from Spanish first round co-leader Alvaro Quirós with a second round 69.

It sent him into the weekend holding a two-shot cushion over Australia’s Jason Day, with Tiger Woods a further stroke behind and back in the hunt for a 15th major after a surging second round 66.

And yet the 21-year-old leader looked perfectly at ease with having a target on his back. Even after a tentative start to the third round, McIlroy rallied with three birdies across the closing six holes to stretch his lead to four strokes heading into Sunday.

The youngster was out on his own ahead of a bunched chasing pack comprising Day, Ángel Cabrera, K.J. Choi and Charl Schwartzel. After 54 holes, McIlroy had shot just three bogeys.

“It’s a great position to be in … I’m finally feeling comfortable on this golf course,” McIlroy told reporters.

“I’m not getting ahead of myself, I know how leads can dwindle away very quickly. I have to go out there, not take anything for granted and go out and play as hard as I’ve played the last three days. If I can do that, hopefully things will go my way.

“We’ll see what happens tomorrow because four shots on this golf course isn’t that much.”

The truth can hurt, and McIlroy was about to prove his assessment of Augusta to be true in the most excruciating way imaginable.

His fourth bogey of the week arrived immediately. Having admitted to expecting some nerves at the first tee, McIlroy sparked a booming opening drive down the fairway, only to miss his putt from five feet.

Three consecutive pars steadied the ship, but Schwartzel had the wind in his sails. A blistering birdie, par, eagle start had seen him draw level at the summit after his third hole.

A subsequent bogey from the South African slowed his charge, as McIlroy clung onto a one-shot lead at the turn from Schwartzel, Cabrera, Choi, and a rampaging Woods, who shot five birdies and an eagle across the front nine to send Augusta into a frenzy.

Despite his dwindling advantage and the raucous Tiger-mania din ahead of him, McIlroy had responded well to another bogey at the 5th hole, draining a brilliant 20-foot putt at the 7th to restore his lead.

The fist pump that followed marked the high-water point of McIlroy’s round, as a sliding start accelerated into full-blown free-fall at the par-four 10th hole.

His tee shot went careening into a tree, ricocheting to settle between the white cabins that separate the main course from the adjacent par-three course. It offered viewers a glimpse at a part of Augusta rarely seen on broadcast, followed by pictures of McIlroy anxiously peering out from behind a tree to track his follow-up shot.

Though his initial escape was successful, yet another collision with a tree and a two-putt on the green saw a stunned McIlroy eventually tap in for a triple bogey. Having led the field one hole and seven shots earlier, he arrived at the 11th tee in seventh.

By the time his tee drive at the 13th plopped into the creek, all thoughts of who might be the recipient of the green jacket had long-since switched away from the anguished youngster. It had taken him seven putts to navigate the previous two greens, as a bogey and a double bogey dropped him to five-under – the score he had held after just 11 holes of the tournament.

Mercifully, the last five holes passed without major incident. A missed putt for birdie from five feet at the final hole summed up McIlroy’s day, though he was given a rousing reception as he left the green.

Mere minutes earlier, the same crowd had erupted as Schwartzel sunk his fourth consecutive birdie to seal his first major title. After starting the day four shots adrift of McIlroy, the South African finished 10 shots ahead of him, and two ahead of second-placed Australian duo Jason Day and Adam Scott.

McIlroy’s eight-over 80 marked the highest score of the round. Having headlined the leaderboard for most of the week, he finished tied-15th.

Tears would flow during a phone call with his parents the following morning, but at his press conference, McIlroy was upbeat.

“I’m very disappointed at the minute, and I’m sure I will be for the next few days, but I’ll get over it,” he said.

“I was leading this golf tournament with nine holes to go, and I just unraveled … It’s a Sunday at a major, what it can do.

“This is my first experience at it, and hopefully the next time I’m in this position I’ll be able to handle it a little better. I didn’t handle it particularly well today obviously, but it was a character-building day … I’ll come out stronger for it.”

Once again, McIlroy would be proven right.

Just eight weeks later in June, McIlroy rampaged to an eight-shot victory at the US Open. Records tumbled in his wake at Congressional, as he shot a tournament record 16-under 268 to become the youngest major winner since Tiger Woods at The Masters in 1997.

The historic victory kickstarted a golden era for McIlroy. After coasting to another eight-shot win at the PGA Championship in 2012, McIlroy became only the third golfer since 1934 to win three majors by the age of 25 with triumph at the 2014 Open Championship.

Before the year was out, he would add his fourth major title with another PGA Championship win.

And much of it was owed to that fateful afternoon at Augusta. In an interview with the BBC in 2015, McIlroy dubbed it “the most important day” of his career.

“If I had not had the whole unravelling, if I had just made a couple of bogeys coming down the stretch and lost by one, I would not have learned as much.

“Luckily, it did not take me long to get into a position like that again when I was leading a major and I was able to get over the line quite comfortably. It was a huge learning curve for me and I needed it, and thankfully I have been able to move on to bigger and better things.

“Looking back on what happened in 2011, it doesn’t seem as bad when you have four majors on your mantelpiece.”

McIlroy’s contentment came with a caveat: it would be “unthinkable” if he did not win The Masters in his career.

Yet as he prepares for his 15th appearance at Augusta National this week, a green jacket remains an elusive missing item from his wardrobe.

Despite seven top-10 finishes in his past 10 Masters outings, the trophy remains the only thing separating McIlroy from joining the ranks of golf immortals to have completed golf’s career grand slam of all four majors in the modern era: Gene Sarazen, Ben Hogan, Gary Player, Jack Nicklaus, and Tiger Woods.

A runner-up finish to Scottie Scheffler last year marked McIlroy’s best finish at Augusta, yet arguably 2011 remains the closest he has ever been to victory. A slow start in 2022 meant McIlroy had begun Sunday’s deciding round 10 shots adrift of the American, who teed off for his final hole with a five-shot lead despite McIlroy’s brilliant 64 finish.

At 33 years old, time is still on his side. Though 2022 extended his major drought to eight years, it featured arguably his best golf since that golden season in 2014.

And as McIlroy knows better than most, things can change quickly at Augusta National.

#369. Walmart hikes outlook as CEO tells CNBC retailer aims to keep prices low despite soaring fuel costs

Walmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce growth ahead of the busy holiday season.

Walmart said global e-commerce sales surged 17% in the fiscal third quarter, driven by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, with Walmart U.S. up 23% and Sam's Club U.S. rising 30%. Its Walmart U.S. advertising business saw a 37% sales increase for the quarter.

Walmart said it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices.

CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the company has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices.

"The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner said in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can."

CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that growth in online orders for Walmart and Sam's Club was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and reduced prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter.

"This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses."

Walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to increase between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared with previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey said Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance.

Walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter ended Oct. 31, the company reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 5.2%.

Adjusting for investment gains and losses, tax matters and reorganization charges, Walmart earned 65 cents per share.

Walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from a year earlier. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount.

Furner also said Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average.

"It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he said.

Sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It said its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise.

In October, Walmart announced it was launching a joint membership option with Walmart+ and Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer stand-alone memberships, as well.

Furner told CNBC the new membership has brought roughly 2 million new people into Sam's Club since its launch in late October. Though the company reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added that it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more."

The company on Thursday said its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter.

The company is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter, the company said it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef.

Rainey said Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start."

The big-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.

Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.

#367. Inspired by Bernie Sanders: A German agency is using US-Style campaigning to boost the left in 2029

"The Goodforces" wants to see a swing to the left in the 2029 German elections. The agency counts New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Bernie Sanders among its inspirations. Could it transform the political landscape?

Red, red, green — those are the party colors of the left-leaning coalition recently formed in the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Now a Berlin-based agency wants to see the same alliance between the center-left Social Democrats, the socialist Left Party, and environmentalist Greens win the 2029 national elections.

The Goodforces wants to help make that a reality with their campaign neunund20 (twenty-nine), taking its cue, in part, from the American left. The agency was set up in response to the rise of the far right across Europe.

Co-founder Patrick Haermeyer told DW that the campaign's aim is "to give people hope and an alternative narrative to: Things are getting worse and worse." He worked as an online organizer for the election team of Bernie Sanders in the US Democratic presidential primaries in 2016 and cites Sanders' "not me, us" campaign as an inspiration.

Neunund20 currently has two strategies: It provides digital space for short-form videos and social media content on political and social topics on Instagram, Tiktok, and Bluesky. At the same time, it tries to connect content creators, activists, NGOs, and political initiatives around shared "progressive" issues.

Users with a particular interest can click to get a link giving them access to archives of relevant social media material that they can then reshare. That feature is modelled on the campaign of New York's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani.

And there are other projects. The Goodforces was recently involved in a tactical voting initiative in the September elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, intended to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from winning an absolute majority. Haermeyer says physical campaigns of that kind are necessary to provide essential "interim victories" en route to the next parliamentary elections.

The Greens and the SPD, the two parties recommended by the app created by the organization, made it over the 5% hurdle and into parliament. The help that they received was declared by each party in the form of a €40,000 ($43,900) donation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The agency sees itself as a kind of Super PAC, modeled on political organizations in the United States that collect money to carry out campaigns without directly supporting a single party or a special candidate.

For Christoph Bieber, political scientist at the University of Duisburg-Essen, the Goodforces is an interesting new type of player on Germany's political scene because it operates outside the country's political parties.

But many of those parties are eyeing the development with disquiet. The far-left, populist, immigration skeptical Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) criticized the Goodforces' intervention in Saxony-Anhalt, telling the newspaper FAZ that it was an "infantilizing, and perhaps even antidemocratic action." The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) called the tool "wrong and intentionally misleading." The FDP failed to clear the threshold, while the BSW only just squeaked in. The AfD gained 43% of the vote and its candidate may soon become Germany's first far-right state premier since the Nazi era.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Haermeyer set up the agency in 2024 along with Peter Jelinek, and both men previously worked for Green Party European Parliament member Michael Bloss. Ahead of that year's European elections, the EU's Green Deal began to come under increasing attack.

That year also ended with the collapse of Germany's first federal coalition between the SPD, Greens, and FDP, after much infighting and attacks from right-wing quarters.

"We noticed that more and more successes and freedoms that we had fought for were being reversed: Things like freedom of movement, border checks, and other things that were coming more and more under fire," Haermeyer told DW. "And we noticed that it was primarily democratic and progressive forces that were being drawn into defensive battles."

The AfD, founded in 2013, already in the age of social media, has successfully targeted younger voters with in its online campaigns. But the older parties, in particular, have struggled. The Goodforces saw a need for support in the online environment and is now seeking to plug this gap.

The social media accounts of the campaign neunund20 contain posts on domestic German topics, such as the current negotiations to form a red-red-green coalition government in Berlin, and the country's new military service law. They also highlight "wins" in Spain in the protests for affordable housing and for US Democrats in the midterms.

Haermeyer stresses that the issues the agency highlights are determined together with a wide range of grassroots organizations and activists. "The campaign is not agreed in conjunction with the SPD, the Left Party, and the Greens," he said.

Agency funding comes from commissions and small donations. Haermeyer says that contributions generally range from $20 to $50.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bieber sees the emergence of non-party campaigning, long an accepted practice in the US, as a bid to compensate for the shortcomings of traditional parties.

"It is an omission of the parties," he said. "For years they have been saying we have to modernize, we have to become more open and get away from rigid membership structures. There are legal regulations governing the organization of political parties in Germany, but perhaps it could be more flexible and open."

The center-left and center-right big-tent parties have been in decline for decades. Membership of the SPD dropped from 943,000 in 1990 to some 348,000 at the end of 2025. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has seen a fall from 750,000 to under 357,000.

Party membership is particularly low in former communist eastern Germany. Centrist parties have also struggled to attract younger voters. A report by the Deutsche Kinder und Jugendstiftung (German Children and Youth Foundation) showed that only 20% of young people felt their concerns were taken seriously in the 2025 German elections and that trust in parties was low.

In the United States, campaign financing comes predominantly from donations, and lobby groups can buy influence by contributing unlimited amounts to super PACs. In Germany, party funding comes, in part, from taxpayers and membership fees, and donations are capped. However, Bieber warns that whereas there are strict rules regarding the disclosure of donors to US Super PACs, these do not exist in Germany.

The political scientist does not believe that US-style campaigning is going to take hold in Germany, but he does see potential dangers: "This could be a door opener to make others consider whether they want to go in this direction in the field of campaigning. And he added: "If it becomes rife, it could lead to a further devaluation of parties and their structures."

#366. Shop Small: Our Favorite Gifts From Independent Businesses (2026)

We get it—Ordering from Amazon is easy. But aside from being community anchors in their respective towns and neighborhoods, small, independent businesses offer some critical things the big guys don’t: curation and specialization. If you don't know anything about stationery, it helps to buy it from someone who lives and breathes fountain pens and Japanese notebooks. You may not want to sort through the millions of toys on Walmart's website, but a mom who really knows toys can help you find just the right gift for just the right age.

For Small Business Saturday, November 28, and throughout the holiday shopping season, consider shopping at an independent business, whether in your own city or via one of the links below. Each store is one that someone on our Reviews team has visited in person or bought something from and loved. Some are in our hometowns, some we happened upon on vacation, and others are places we regularly shop. Here’s what we’d buy.

This locally owned Greenpoint shop is recommended by Gear editor Julian Chokkattu as being a mecca for writers and sketchers. Its brick-lined walls hold shelves’ worth of every type of pen, paper, and notebook imaginable, with an emphasis on Asian stationery like Hobonichi's popular Techo paper planners (which we highly recommend). Yoseka’s Shop store allows customers to buy pens individually, so you can put together a sampler or select only the colors you know your recipient will want.

• Stalogy Editor's Series 365Days Notebook: $28

Founded in 1948 by Edith and Brian Heath, Heath Ceramics still makes the same ceramic dinnerware, vases, and tiles the founders made back then, which are fully back in style now due to their midcentury modern flair. As a fifth-generation San Francisco Bay Area native, I still have a set of green Heath cereal bowls my grandmother bought when the Sausalito showroom—which is still in operation and is still attached to the factory—was relatively new.

WIRED operations manager Scott Gilbertson loves this locally owned toy store and community space known for its quirky and original toys, from vintage-inspired matchbox stuffies to keychain-sized digital cameras and retro candy. (There’s also a sister location, Clubhouse Kid and Craft, just outside of Atlanta, though that one has different owners.) As a side note, I knew few kids—including my own—who haven't loved Magna-Tiles.

Part of the growing “slow fashion” movement, this vintage-inspired boutique sells shirts, pants, jackets, and even underwear made painstakingly by hand right in Brooklyn and meant to last a lifetime. It's mostly men's garments online and accessories like the waxed-cotton pouch above, though there are some women's cashmere coats in the physical store.

• Mongolian Cashmere Prayer Slippers: $105

Though I live in San Diego, one of my best friends lives in the Dallas area near McKinney. Walking around the adorable historic downtown is one of our favorite pastimes when I visit, and a shop we always find ourselves back at is Fair and Square Imports. The shop is focused on fair trade goods, working with artisan cooperatives and Fair Trade partners from around the world. As you peruse the shop, you’ll find all kinds of home goods, ranging from ornaments for the holidays, beautiful home pieces, bath goods, kids’ books, and so much more. On my last visit, I bought a massage stone and bath salts, while my friend bought flavored honey and a fantastically scented lotion. You won’t find all the fun goods online that they have in store, but you can shop an impressive range of their well-priced goods online. —Nena Farrell

Owned by a local color designer, this downtown Portland gift shop is hard to miss with its cheery window displays and decidedly mod vibe. It features all manner of colorful art and gifts by independent artists; Woonwinkel's website lets you sort selections by Black-owned, POC-owned, USA-made, and eco-friendly, though the Shop site does not. In any case, if you or a giftee likes bright, stylish things with lots of color, this is the place.

When you choose made-to-order footwear from Crown Northampton, it feels like stepping backward in time, pun intended. You’re supporting a family business dating back to 1908, now in its fifth generation of stewardship; managing director Chris Woodford is the great-great-grandson of founder Earnest Woodford. And you’re investing in stellar craftsmanship—true buy-it-for-life goods. These are premium boots made by hand with the highest-quality materials (like Horween Chromexcel leather) and techniques (stitchdown construction), with zero outsourcing. Most things simply aren’t made this way nowadays. Most other shoes aren’t initialed in pen to note that they passed inspection. But the Woodfords are proud to keep the tradition alive. —Cooper Fleishman

• Woodford Desert Boot—Snuff Kudu Suede: $424

Hamilton’s iconic field watch is perfect for nearly any setting, hardy enough to endure toddler mealtime or outdoor adventures but dashing enough to pair well with office attire. Watch nerds call it GADA—a “go anywhere, do anything” style. On one hand, it’s the last timepiece you’ll ever need to buy. But on the other hand, what’s the fun in that? A great field watch is a gateway to all sorts of fun and distinctive wristwear at any price, much of which can be found at Windup Watch Shop in Brooklyn. My friend Nick Coe, who runs the menswear brand network Kutoku, calls it a true enthusiast-first shop. While other retailers can feel intimidating and exclusive, Windup welcomes all. There’s a terrific range of brands, products, and prices—check out the wall clocks!—with approachable service, a high taste level, and an even higher bar for quality. If you love watches—or if you want to love watches but you’re afraid you can’t afford to—Windup is the perfect place to start your collection. —Cooper Fleishman

• Windup Watch Shop x Caravelle by Bulova Sea Hunter: $425

• Hamilton Khaki Field Mechanical 36mm: $725

• Timex Atelier Chronograph Automatic 42mm: $2,100

This hip, brick-lined design shop in Melrose Market draws you (OK, maybe just me) in with its display of houseplants, but it's also a hot spot for housewares, stationery, interesting soaps, and cool, high-end casualwear like vintage-cut plain tees and Japanese selvedge denim. The physical store also offers a host of creative DIY workshops on topics like working with natural dyes or making kokedamas (moss ball planters).

Founded in 2006 by James Beard Award-winning cookbook author Mark Bitterman, the Meadow features some gourmet foods and gifts here and there, but the focus is on one thing: salt. Exotic flavored salt, finishing salt, Himalayan salt cooking blocks, and chocolate bars with fleur de sel are all featured both in-store (three locations in Portland, one in SoHo) and online. I have shopped in-store many times, and my favorite purchases are always the smoked salts, like the Halen Môn smoked salt from Wales, or the sea salt cold-smoked over cherry wood.

• The Meadow Salted Caramel Milk Chocolate: $12

My wife’s go-to bag is this buttery-soft full-grain leather ring bag that can be worn in several ways: crossbody, shoulder, or handheld. It’s made by our local Hyer Goods, whose founder, Dana Cohen, shows a deep commitment to sustainable luxury by adapting surplus leather from well-known fashion houses’ Italian tanneries. We love the classic Ring Bag, and we fight over the wool whenever it’s chilly. —Cooper Fleishman
